Charge in motion

26.0 — Setting the Charges in Motion

In Chapters 22 through 25, we built a powerful framework for electrostatics — charges at rest. We learned how charges create electric fields, how Gauss’s Law relates fields to enclosed charge, how electric potential provides a scalar energy landscape, and how capacitors store energy in the field itself. In every case, the charges were stationary.

Now we set the charges in motion.

When a potential difference is maintained across a conductor — by a battery, for example — the electric field inside drives free charges through the material, producing a continuous flow called electric current. This chapter introduces the vocabulary of circuits: current, resistance, resistivity, and electrical power.

The story begins with Alessandro Volta (1745–1827), whose voltaic pile first provided a steady source of potential difference. Before Volta, experiments with static electricity produced spectacular sparks but no sustained flow. With the battery, sustained current became possible, and André-Marie Ampère (1775–1836) quickly developed a mathematical framework for the magnetic effects of current — work we will encounter in later chapters.

But it was Georg Simon Ohm (1789–1854) who made the crucial connection between current and voltage: the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it. His law, published in 1827, was initially rejected — critics thought it “too simple” to be fundamental. Ohm lost his teaching position and spent years in obscurity before vindication.

“The force of the current in a galvanic circuit is directly as the sum of all the tensions, and inversely as the entire length of the circuit.” — Georg Ohm, Die galvanische Kette (1827)

*Personal note: Ohm’s story is a reminder that simplicity in physics is a feature, not a flaw. His law is one of the most used equations in all of engineering, and it was nearly lost because it seemed “too obvious.”

26.1 — Electric Current

Definition of Current

When charges flow through a conductor, we define the electric current \(I\) as the rate at which charge passes through a cross-sectional area. If a net charge \(\Delta Q\) passes through in time \(\Delta t\), the average current is \(I_\text{avg} = \Delta Q/\Delta t\). The instantaneous current is:

\[\boxed{I \equiv \frac{dQ}{dt}}\]

The SI unit of current is the ampere (A), named after André-Marie Ampère: \(1\ \text{A} = 1\ \text{C/s}\). The ampere is an SI base unit — the coulomb is defined as the charge transported by 1 A in 1 second.

Direction of Current

By convention, conventional current flows in the direction positive charges would move — from high potential to low potential, in the direction of the electric field. In metals, the actual carriers are electrons moving opposite to the conventional current. Both descriptions produce the same physical effects, so we consistently use conventional current.

*Personal note: This convention was established by Benjamin Franklin before the electron was discovered. By the time J.J. Thomson identified the electron in 1897, it was too deeply embedded to change. Every circuit diagram in the world still follows Franklin’s guess.

The Water-Pipe Analogy

Electric current is often compared to water flowing through pipes. The analogy is imperfect but useful for building intuition:

Water Analogy Electrical Quantity Symbol Unit
Flow rate (gallons/min) Current \(I\) A (ampere)
Pressure difference Potential difference \(\Delta V\) V (volt)
Pipe restriction/friction Resistance \(R\) \(\Omega\) (ohm)
Pump Battery (EMF source) \(\mathcal{E}\) V

More pressure (voltage) drives more flow (current); a narrower or longer pipe (higher resistance) restricts flow.

26.2 — Microscopic Model: Drift Velocity

Charge Carriers in a Conductor

What happens inside a wire when current flows? The wire contains an enormous number of free electrons — roughly one per atom in a metal like copper. We describe the conductor by:

  • Number density \(n\): the number of mobile charge carriers per unit volume (m\(^{-3}\))
  • Charge \(q\): the charge of each carrier (for electrons, \(q = e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\) C)
  • Cross-sectional area \(A\): the wire’s cross-section (m\(^2\))

Derivation of Current from Drift Velocity

Consider a cylindrical segment of wire with cross-sectional area \(A\). In a time interval \(\Delta t\), carriers moving with drift velocity \(v_d\) sweep out a cylinder of length \(\Delta x = v_d\Delta t\).

The charge in this volume is \(\Delta Q = (nAv_d\Delta t)q\), so:

\[\boxed{I = nqv_dA}\]

The current density \(J\) is the current per unit area:

\[\boxed{J = \frac{I}{A} = nqv_d}\]

Random Motion vs. Drift

Without an applied electric field, the free electrons in a metal are not stationary — they zip around at enormous thermal speeds, on the order of \(10^6\) m/s at room temperature. However, their motion is random in every direction, so the average velocity over all electrons is zero. No net charge transport occurs.

When an external electric field \(\vec{E}\) is applied, each electron experiences a force \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\) that gives it a slight bias in one direction between collisions with lattice ions. The result is a tiny net drift velocity \(\vec{v}_d\) superimposed on the random thermal motion. The drift speed is vastly smaller than the thermal speed, as the following example shows.

Example: Drift Speed in a Copper Wire

A 12-gauge copper wire (\(A = 3.31 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)) carries \(I = 10.0\) A. Copper: density \(\rho_m = 8920\) kg/m\(^3\), molar mass \(M = 0.0635\) kg/mol. One free electron per atom.

Number density: \(n = N_A\rho_m/M = (6.022 \times 10^{23})(8920)/0.0635 = 8.46 \times 10^{28}\) m\(^{-3}\)

Drift speed:

\[v_d = \frac{I}{nqA} = \frac{10.0}{(8.46 \times 10^{28})(1.602 \times 10^{-19})(3.31 \times 10^{-6})}\]

\[\boxed{v_d = 2.23 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m/s} \approx 0.223\ \text{mm/s}}\]

Interpretation: The drift speed is astonishingly slow — less than a quarter of a millimeter per second! At this rate, an electron would take about 4.5 hours to travel 1 meter through the wire. Yet when you flip a light switch, the light comes on almost instantly. How? The electric field propagates through the wire at nearly the speed of light, setting all electrons in motion almost simultaneously. It is the signal that travels fast, not the individual electrons.

*Personal note: Think of a garden hose already full of water. When you open the nozzle, water comes out the far end immediately — not because any individual water molecule traveled the length of the hose, but because the pressure wave propagated quickly. Current works the same way.

26.3 — Resistance, Ohm’s Law, and Resistivity

Microscopic Ohm’s Law

For many materials, the current density is proportional to the electric field:

\[\vec{J} = \sigma\vec{E}\]

where \(\sigma\) is the conductivity of the material (units: S/m). This is Ohm’s Law in microscopic form.

Deriving Macroscopic Ohm’s Law

For a uniform conductor of length \(\ell\) and cross-sectional area \(A\), with potential difference \(\Delta V\):

The uniform field is \(E = \Delta V/\ell\) and \(J = I/A\). Substituting into \(J = \sigma E\):

\[\frac{I}{A} = \sigma\frac{\Delta V}{\ell} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \Delta V = \frac{\ell}{\sigma A}I = RI\]

We define resistance:

\[\boxed{R \equiv \frac{\Delta V}{I}} \qquad \text{units: ohm}\ (\Omega) = \text{V/A}\]

This gives Ohm’s Law in its most familiar form:

\[\boxed{\Delta V = IR}\]

A material is ohmic if \(R\) is constant (linear \(I\)-\(\Delta V\) curve). Most metals are ohmic. Non-ohmic devices — diodes, semiconductors, heated filaments — have resistance that varies with voltage or temperature.

Resistance from Geometry and Resistivity

Since \(R = \ell/(\sigma A)\), we write resistance in terms of resistivity \(\rho = 1/\sigma\) (\(\Omega \cdot \text{m}\)):

\[\boxed{R = \rho\frac{\ell}{A}}\]

Resistance depends on three things: the material (\(\rho\)), the length (\(\ell\)), and the cross-sectional area (\(A\)). Longer conductors have more resistance; thicker conductors have less.

Resistivities of Common Materials

Material Resistivity (\(\Omega \cdot \text{m}\)) Classification
Silver \(1.59 \times 10^{-8}\) Conductor
Copper \(1.7 \times 10^{-8}\) Conductor
Aluminum \(2.82 \times 10^{-8}\) Conductor
Tungsten \(5.6 \times 10^{-8}\) Conductor
Nichrome \(1.00 \times 10^{-6}\) Conductor (alloy)
Carbon \(3.5 \times 10^{-5}\) Semiconductor
Germanium \(0.46\) Semiconductor
Silicon \(2.3 \times 10^{3}\) Semiconductor
Glass \(10^{10}\) to \(10^{14}\) Insulator
Fused quartz \(75 \times 10^{16}\) Insulator

All values at \(20°\text{C}\). The range spans roughly 24 orders of magnitude — no other material property varies so widely.

Example: The Resistance of Nichrome Wire

The radius of 22-gauge Nichrome wire is 0.32 mm. (A) Resistance per unit length:

\[\frac{R}{\ell} = \frac{\rho}{\pi r^2} = \frac{1.00 \times 10^{-6}}{\pi(0.32 \times 10^{-3})^2} = \boxed{3.1\ \Omega/\text{m}}\]

(B) Current when 10 V is applied across 1.0 m: \(R = 3.1\ \Omega\), so \(I = \Delta V/R = 10/3.1 = \boxed{3.2\ \text{A}}\).

Nichrome’s resistivity is ~60 times that of copper, which is why it is used in heating elements.

26.4 — Temperature Dependence and the Drude Model

Temperature Dependence of Resistivity

For most metals, resistivity increases approximately linearly with temperature:

\[\boxed{\rho = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]} \qquad \text{equivalently,} \qquad R = R_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]\]

where \(\alpha\) is the temperature coefficient of resistivity (units: \(°\text{C}^{-1}\)).

Material \(\alpha\) (\(°\text{C}^{-1}\)) Material \(\alpha\) (\(°\text{C}^{-1}\))
Copper \(3.9 \times 10^{-3}\) Carbon \(-0.5 \times 10^{-3}\)
Tungsten \(4.5 \times 10^{-3}\) Germanium \(-48 \times 10^{-3}\)
Nichrome \(0.4 \times 10^{-3}\) Silicon \(-75 \times 10^{-3}\)

Metals (positive \(\alpha\)): higher temperature means more lattice vibrations, more electron scattering, higher resistivity. Semiconductors (negative \(\alpha\)): higher temperature frees more carriers, which outweighs increased scattering.

*Personal note: This is why incandescent bulbs draw a surge of current at turn-on. A cold tungsten filament has much lower resistance; at operating temperature (~\(2800°\text{C}\)), its resistance is ~10 times the room-temperature value. The inrush current is why bulbs most often burn out at the moment you flip the switch.

The Drude Model

In 1900, Paul Drude modeled conduction electrons as a classical gas accelerated by \(\vec{E}\) and scattered by lattice ions. If the mean time between collisions is \(\tau\), each electron acquires drift velocity \(v_d = (qE/m_e)\tau\). Substituting into \(J = nqv_d\) and comparing with \(J = \sigma E\) gives:

\[\boxed{\sigma = \frac{nq^2\tau}{m_e}}\]

This connects measurable conductivity to microscopic quantities — carrier density \(n\), charge \(q\), mass \(m_e\), and scattering time \(\tau\). The Drude model is classical and incomplete, but it correctly predicts Ohm’s Law and gives the right order of magnitude for \(\sigma\).

Superconductors

In 1911, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered that mercury cooled below \(T_c = 4.15\) K has exactly zero resistance — a phenomenon called superconductivity. A current in a superconducting loop flows indefinitely. The discovery of high-temperature cuprate superconductors in the 1980s (YBa\(_2\)Cu\(_3\)O\(_7\) at 92 K, cooled with liquid nitrogen rather than liquid helium) was revolutionary. The current record is 134 K — still far below room temperature, and raising \(T_c\) remains a great open problem.

26.5 — Electrical Power

Power Delivered to a Circuit Element

Consider a battery (\(\Delta V\)) connected to a resistor (\(R\)).

As charge \(dQ\) moves through the battery, it gains energy \(dU = dQ \cdot \Delta V\). The rate of energy delivery is:

\[P = \frac{dU}{dt} = \frac{dQ}{dt}\Delta V\]

\[\boxed{P = I\Delta V}\]

For an ohmic resistor (\(\Delta V = IR\)):

\[\boxed{P = I^2R = \frac{(\Delta V)^2}{R}}\]

All three forms give power in watts (W = J/s). Use \(P = I^2R\) when current is known; use \(P = (\Delta V)^2/R\) when voltage is known.

Example: Power in an Electric Heater

A heater applies 120 V across Nichrome wire with \(R = 8.00\ \Omega\).

\[I = \frac{\Delta V}{R} = \frac{120}{8.00} = 15.0\ \text{A}\]

\[P = I^2R = (15.0)^2(8.00) = \boxed{1.80\ \text{kW}}\]

A typical space heater — 1.8 kW of electrical power, all converted to thermal energy.

The Kilowatt-Hour and Power Transmission

The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the energy unit on electric bills: \(1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6\ \text{J}\). Despite its name, it is an energy unit (power \(\times\) time).

Power lost in transmission lines goes as \(P_\text{loss} = I^2R_\text{wire}\). Since \(P = I\Delta V\), transmitting at high voltage reduces \(I\) and dramatically cuts \(I^2R\) losses — this is why power lines operate at hundreds of thousands of volts and transformers step the voltage down near your home.

26.6 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Electric current \(I = dQ/dt\) is the rate of charge flow. Unit: ampere (A = C/s). Conventional current flows in the direction positive charges would move.

  2. Drift velocity: \(I = nqv_dA\). Drift speeds are tiny (~0.2 mm/s in copper); the electric field signal propagates at nearly \(c\).

  3. Ohm’s Law: \(\Delta V = IR\). Resistance \(R = \Delta V/I\) is constant for ohmic materials.

  4. Resistivity: \(R = \rho\ell/A\). Resistivity is a material property spanning 24 orders of magnitude.

  5. Temperature dependence: \(\rho = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]\). Metals: positive \(\alpha\); semiconductors: negative \(\alpha\).

  6. Power: \(P = I\Delta V = I^2R = (\Delta V)^2/R\).

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Current \(I = dQ/dt\)
Drift velocity relation \(I = nqv_dA\)
Ohm’s Law (microscopic) \(\vec{J} = \sigma\vec{E}\)
Ohm’s Law (macroscopic) \(\Delta V = IR\)
Resistance from geometry \(R = \rho\ell/A\)
Temperature dependence \(\rho = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]\)
Power \(P = I\Delta V = I^2R = (\Delta V)^2/R\)

Looking Ahead

In Chapter 27, we introduce DC circuits — networks of resistors and batteries analyzed using Kirchhoff’s rules. We will derive the series and parallel combination rules for resistors and bring capacitors and resistors together in RC circuits, where the time constant \(\tau = RC\) governs exponential charge and discharge.

*With current and resistance in hand, we now have the vocabulary to read a circuit diagram. Kirchhoff’s rules will give us the grammar.
